Stablish
STAB-lish
verb
The older aphetic form of establish, from Old French establir, from Latin stabilire, “to make firm,” from stabilis, “standing fast,” from stare, “to stand.” To make stable; to fix; to settle so that a thing cannot be moved.

Biblical Definition

To stablish is to make a thing stand — to fix, settle, and secure it so that it holds. The Authorized Version keeps the older short form beside establish, and it falls most often on the doctrine our age most needs. Note who does the stablishing. Paul prays “to the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God” (1Th 3:13); he asks that God “comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work” (2Th 2:17); he blesses the One “that is of power to stablish you according to my gospel” (Rom 16:25); he says flatly, “he which stablisheth us with you in Christ…is God” (2Co 1:21). Peter says the same after the furnace: “the God of all grace…after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you” (1Pe 5:10). Four verbs, one Actor. The believer’s perseverance is not the strength of his grip upon Christ but the strength of Christ’s grip upon him; the saints continue because God stablishes, and God stablishes because He has covenanted to do it. So the psalmist prays for the ground of it: “Stablish thy word unto thy servant, who is devoted to thy fear” (Psa 119:38). The word stablishes the man because God stablishes the word; and the throne of David’s greater Son is stablished for ever (2Sa 7:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

To make firm or stable; to fix; to settle; to confirm so that a thing cannot be moved.

expand to see more

STABLISH, to fix; to settle in a state for permanence; to make firm.

The aphetic older form of establish; the AV uses both.

From Latin stabilire, from stabilis, “standing fast” (stare, to stand).

In the epistles God is nearly always the One who stablishes (2Co 1:21).

Peter joins it to perfecting, strengthening, and settling (1Pe 5:10).

Key Scripture

1Th 3:13 — "To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints."

2Th 2:17 — "Comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work."

1Pe 5:10 — "But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you."

Psa 119:38 — "Stablish thy word unto thy servant, who is devoted to thy fear."

Modern Corruption

The word is passive in the saint and active in God; modern religion reverses it and hands the believer the job of holding on.

expand to see more

Two errors meet at this word. The first is the free-will revivalism that makes perseverance a task laid on the convert: he must keep himself, maintain his decision, hold his ground, and if he slips the whole work collapses. On that scheme a Christian is stablished only as long as his nerve lasts, and assurance is impossible by definition. The second error is the mirror image — a bare “once saved, always saved” that severs the promise from the process, as though a man could be stablished without ever standing, secured without ever being sanctified. Scripture will have neither. It says God stablishes, and it says the stablished walk in every good word and work; the same passage holds both because the God who ordains the end ordains the means.

The Reformed answer is the perseverance of the saints, and it is only the doctrine of these verses read plainly. Peter puts the suffering first and the stablishing after — after that ye have suffered a while — because God’s ordinary way of making a soul stand is to knock out every prop but Himself. Paul asks that hearts be stablished unblameable in holiness at the coming of Christ, which is to say that the saint’s final standing is already the object of an apostolic prayer God has bound Himself to answer. The believer’s comfort is therefore not in the firmness of his hold but in the faithfulness of the Holder: “the foundation of God standeth sure” (2Ti 2:19), and He that began a good work will perform it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

To make firm and unmoveable; in the epistles, always God’s work upon His people.

expand to see more

Stablish — older form of establish, Latin stabilire, “to make firm.”

The root is stare, “to stand” — a stablished man stands.

God is the subject: He stablisheth us in Christ (2Co 1:21).

It sits beside perfect, strengthen, settle in 1Pe 5:10.

The Word stablishes the servant because God stablishes the Word (Psa 119:38).

Usage

"He may stablish your hearts: the praying apostle asks God for what no convert can do for himself."

"Stablish, strengthen, settle — three words for one covenant faithfulness."

"A saint stands, but he does not stand by standing; he stands because God stablishes."
